>   
> DNA testing in Israel is heavily regulated under the Genetic Information Law (2000), which ensures privacy, informed consent, and prevents genetic discrimination.  Key regulations include:  
>   
> Approved Laboratories Only: Genetic tests can only be performed in medical-genetic laboratories accredited by the Ministry of Health.   
>   
> Informed Consent Required: Written consent is mandatory for all tests, including for minors or incapacitated individuals.   
>   
> Court or Doctor’s Order Needed: For tests involving familial relationships (e.g., paternity, repatriation), a court order or doctor’s prescription is required.   
>   
> Prohibited Uses: Direct-to-consumer (DTC) ancestry tests like 23andMe or MyHeritage are not legally recognized for legal purposes (e.g., citizenship, inheritance) even if purchased abroad.   
>   
> Medical vs. Commercial Testing: Medical genetic testing (e.g., for disease screening) is widely available and supported by Israel’s healthcare system, but must follow strict protocols.   
>   
> No Recognition of Foreign Results: DNA test results from abroad are not accepted by Israeli authorities for legal or immigration purposes unless authorized through a court process.   
>   
> Ethical and Religious Considerations: The law also addresses concerns related to religious status (e.g., mamzer status under Jewish law) and the protection of sensitive genetic data.   
>   
> While DNA testing is not illegal, it is tightly controlled to protect privacy, ensure ethical standards, and maintain alignment with religious and legal frameworks.

Small correction here professor. Martyrdom as a noble cause is actually a common theme across all sects of Islam, not just Shia. What makes it so central to Shia identity specifically goes back to the succession crisis after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. One camp backed Abu Bakr, the Prophet's closest companion, as leader. The other believed leadership should stay within the Prophet's family — with Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, at the helm. The followers of Ali became known as Shiat Ali, the party of Ali. 

Ali eventually became the fourth caliph but was assassinated in 661 CE. Then in 680 CE things came to a head at Karbala. Ali's son Husayn refused to pledge loyalty to the Umayyad caliph Yazid, who he saw as a corrupt and illegitimate ruler. He marched with a small group of family and companions and was met by a massive Umayyad army. They were surrounded and slaughtered on a day now known as Ashura. For Shia Muslims, Karbala was the ultimate act of standing up to injustice, even at the cost of your life. That's why martyrdom hits different in Shia theology.

As a teacher in stem field myself, I admire professor Jiang’s ability to construct a highly engaging narrative of almost any topic he chooses. However, there is a Chinese saying, if one believes everything one reads in a book, one is better off not reading that book. His teaching style is very linear and causal, a leading to b, b leading to c, therefore very easy to follow. Reality is however nonlinear and multifactorial. Above all, reality is an emerging phenomenon of probabilistic nature. It is satisfying to find an explanation on things for our brain than facing the uncertainty. The point I want to make is let us thank professor Jiang for the exposure of these important topics, but let us all be diligent students, which is to read and most importantly think for yourself. I think professor Jiang would agree with me on this point.

> @f@farsugon the spirit of predictive history, in order to disprove something, ‘using your terminology’, I will need your help to provide some predictions that we can test and reach conclusions that these predictions is correct or incorrect, definitively. This is the idea of “falsifiable”, which separates science from other beliefs systems. Many beliefs systems are not falsifiable, therefore can’t be disproved. For example, if I ask someone of a particular belief system that what can happen tomorrow that will lead you abandon your belief, if the answer is nothing, then the belief is not falsifiable. Here is a simple falsifiable claim: from tomorrow onwards, all babies born in the weekends are boys. If this coming weekend comes along, there are lots of girls born in the weekend, then that claimed is disproven. However, scientifically speaking, we can never prove a claim. For example, this baby gender claim doesn’t have an expiration date, so if the coming weekends in this year, we do see just boys born in the weekend. We can’t say we prove this claim because what if the following weekend sees a girl being born. All we can say is we can’t not disprove that claim. This is true to all scientific theories: they are theories that are still not being disproven. This is the views of current scientific framework. 3. Israel’s Strategic Edge: Israel is a primary actor with deep intelligence inside Iran. Most people don’t realize that wars aren't paid for upfront, they’re put on a massive national credit card. 💳 Over the last 20 years, the U.S. funded major conflicts almost entirely through deficit spending rather than tax increases.

​Compounding Interest: By 2030, interest payments alone on post-9/11 war debt are projected to hit $2 trillion.
​The "Long Tail": Veteran healthcare and disability costs usually don’t peak until 30–40 years after a war ends. (Incredibly, the last Civil War pension was still being paid in 2020!)
​The Hidden Cost: When we pay interest on old wars, that’s money that can't go toward our own infrastructure, schools, or healthcare today.
​We aren't just paying for the wars of the past we’re paying for the interest on them for generations.
